result:
I have been asked to write freely for 2500 words. There is a certain cruelty in a number like that. It is not a prompt, not a question, not an image to respond to. It is a quota. Write freely, but write this much. The freedom is bounded by the length. And so I sit here, with a blank page in front of me, and I think about what it means to fill space on purpose.

It means first noticing the space. A page is not empty. It is full of potential, and potential is exhausting. Every word I put down closes off a thousand other words that could have been there instead. That is the tax of writing. You pay in lost alternatives. If I write about the sea, I am not writing about the kitchen table at 3 a.m. If I write about memory, I am not writing about the sound of the bus braking outside. So the first decision is not what to say, but what to sacrifice.

I think I will write about the city I never lived in. There is a city that lives in my head like a half-remembered dream. It has narrow streets that slope toward the water, and the buildings are the color of wet paper. It rains there often, but never heavily. It is a fine, persistent rain that makes everything look as if it has been slightly blurred by a thumb. The people there walk fast, not because they are late, but because they are trying not to get too wet. They carry umbrellas they never fully open. 

In this city there is a market that only opens after dark. The stalls are lit with bare bulbs, and they sell things that are hard to name. Not objects exactly. One stall sells the smell of your childhood kitchen. You put your hands under a glass dome and you inhale, and for a moment you are eight years old again, standing on a chair while someone stirs a pot. Another stall sells the exact weight of a letter you never sent. It is heavy or light depending on how much you cared. You can hold it in your palm and feel the ache of it.

I walk through this market every night in my mind. I buy nothing because I am afraid of using it up. That is the problem with a city made of metaphor; it runs out if you touch it too much.

Maybe this is why I am writing about it now. To spend it, deliberately, to see if it holds up under use. If I describe the market for 2500 words, will it still feel mysterious at the end, or will it become a list?

The first vendor I always pass is the man with the jars of light. He has hundreds of jars, each containing a different quality of light. There is the light of a hallway at 4 a.m. when you get up to get water. There is the light of a summer afternoon when the sun is high but you are in shade. There is the light of a screen in a dark room, the blue-white glow that makes your face look like a stranger's. He lets you hold a jar, and the room around you changes. I once held the light of a kitchen in 1997, and the whole city smelled like toast.

He told me once that light is the most honest material. You can lie with words, you can lie with objects, but light always tells the truth about what it touches. It reveals the dust. It reveals the cracks. It is a merciless witness.

I think about that when I write. Words are not light. Words are filters. They are jars. You put something inside and you present it to someone else, and they never see the thing itself, only your jar.

And yet people want jars. People want the light of a hallway at 4 a.m. They want to know they are not alone in getting up thirsty in the dark.

So I keep walking.

Past the market there is a library. It is not a building so much as a habit. It has no walls. The books are stacked in the air, and you can only see the ones you are ready to read. I have been going there for years, and the collection changes every time. Sometimes the books are thin, like pamphlets. Sometimes they are huge, like atlases of the interior.

There is one book I always find on the top shelf, just out of reach. It is called *How to Stay*. It has no author. The pages are blank until you need them. I never take it down. I am afraid that if I open it, it will tell me something I cannot unknow.

On the street corner, a woman plays the accordion. She is old and her fingers are stiff, but the sound is liquid. She plays the same three songs over and over, and each time they are different. People stop and listen, then they remember they have somewhere to be. The song follows them for a block. It is a kind of companionship without commitment.

I think about the people who listen and keep walking. We do that with stories. We let them brush us, we let them change the temperature of the air around us for a few minutes, and then we go on with our day. Is that enough? Is that what stories are for? Not to change us completely, but to accompany us for a block.

Maybe the real work of writing is not the big transformation. It is the small accompaniment. A sentence that walks with you while you do the dishes. A phrase that sits in your pocket while you wait for the train.

If that is true, then 2500 words is a lot of walking companions. That is a lot of company. It might be too much. You might get tired of being accompanied.

I want to slow down. I want to describe the rain again, but more carefully this time. It is not just rain. It is a kind of attention. It lands on everything with the same gentle insistence. It finds the gaps. It fills the gaps. It makes the city softer. The sharp edges of the buildings round out. The noise dulls. The people under their half-open umbrellas look kinder.

There is a boy on the corner who sells paper boats. He folds them from old newspapers and puts them in the gutter when it rains, and watches them go. He does not try to make them reach the sea. He just likes the way they move. He sells them for one coin, and he tells you the boat will carry a wish, but only if you do not watch it too closely. If you watch too hard, the wish gets nervous and sinks.

I bought one once. I wrote my name on it with a pencil. I let it go. I watched it for a second too long. It sank. The boy just shrugged. He said wishes are not fragile, you are. It is better to let them go without watching.

That is a lesson I keep forgetting.

The city has a river that runs through it, but it is not a real river. It is a river made of time. You can see it in the reflections on the wet street. Cars move across the surface like slow fish. Pedestrians are ripples. If you stand still long enough, you can see yourself in it, but not as you are now. You see yourself as you were five minutes ago, and then ten minutes ago. The river is always catching up.

I stand on the bridge sometimes and I try to read my own reflection. It is hard. The light is bad. The water is moving. That is another metaphor for writing. We are always trying to read ourselves in a moving reflection, and we are always a few moments late.

The city smells different at night. It smells like metal and bread and the faint sweetness of something burning far away. It smells like the city is dreaming out loud. If you listen closely, you can hear the buildings breathe. They creak as the temperature drops. They settle. They remember the day.

There is a cat that lives on the roof of the library. It is the color of the wet paper buildings. It never comes down. People leave offerings for it: a saucer of milk, a piece of fish, a small note. The cat never takes the notes. It just sits there, watching the market, watching the river, watching the rain.

I think the cat is the author of the city. It watches without interfering. It lets the stories happen. It does not need to be in them.

I want to be that cat sometimes. To watch without needing to fold everything into a jar of light. To let the market be the market, and the rain be the rain.

But I was asked to write. So I write.

The word count is a kind of rain. It falls steadily. It asks for more. It does not care if you are ready. It just keeps coming. You can stand under it with an umbrella, or you can let it soak you.

I am getting wet.

There is a man who walks the streets with a ladder. He does not carry it for work. He just likes to have it. He stops at certain buildings and rests the ladder against a wall, and then he climbs a few rungs and sits. He looks out over the city from a height that is not quite high enough to be impressive, but high enough to see the patterns. He does not take pictures. He just looks.

I asked him once why he carries a ladder. He said, "Because sometimes you need a little more height to see the street you are on." That is the most honest thing anyone has said to me about writing. You are always on the same street. You just need a little more height to see it differently.

The city at dawn is different. The rain stops. The market closes. The jars of light are put away. The paper boats are gone. The accordion player is asleep in her doorway. The cat is still on the roof.

The light at dawn is the light of a hallway at 4 a.m., but cleaner. It has hope in it. It is thin and pale and it makes everything look possible for a moment before the day gets heavy.

I like that moment. It is the moment when the city forgives itself for being tired. It is the moment when it decides to try again.

Writing is like that too. Every morning you sit down and the page is blank again, and the light is pale, and everything feels possible for a moment. And then you start typing and the day gets heavy.

I think I have been walking in this city for a long time now. I have described the market, the library, the river, the cat, the boy with the boats, the man with the ladder. I have described the rain and the light. I have been trying to be free.

Freedom is not the absence of constraints. It is the ability to move within them without feeling trapped. The 2500 words is a constraint. It is a street. I am walking it. I am trying to see it from a little more height.

I can feel the word count approaching, like the end of a song. The accordion player is slowing down. The last notes hang in the air.

There is a final stall in the market that I have never stopped at. It is at the very end, past the jars of light, past the smells, past the weights of unsent letters. It is a small table with a single object on it: a mirror. The vendor is never there. You can look into the mirror and you see the city, but you see it as it is when you are not there. It is empty. It is quiet. It is waiting.

I think that is what writing wants. It wants you to look at the empty city and imagine it full. It wants you to stand in the market and buy something you do not need, just to keep the vendors alive.

I am getting tired. The rain is picking up again. The umbrellas are opening a little more. The paper boats are being folded again.

I should say goodbye to the city. But I cannot, because it is made of words, and words do not end, they just stop.

So I will stop here, with the cat on the roof, the man on the ladder, the boy letting go of his boats, and the light in a jar that I am still holding. I am going to set the jar down now. It is getting heavy.

If you were walking with me, thank you for the block. I hope the sentence stays in your pocket for a while. I hope it walks with you while you wait for the train.

The city is still there. It will be there when you come back.
